newsitem.title: UK: WEEK AHEAD-U.S. rates, EMU policy under spotlight.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD-U.S. rates, EMU policy under spotlight.

text.p: Financial markets have a critical week ahead, with dealers and investors set to pounce on key decisions by European Union authorities and Federal Reserve policy makers, analysts said on Friday.
EU finance directors and central bank governors were due to gather in Dublin on Saturday for an "Ecofin" summit on moves towards European economic and monetary union (EMU).
Soon after markets digest the results of that meeting, they will be confronted with a Federal Open Market Committee meeting on Tuesday, where many expect a U.S. interest rate rise.

By the end of the week, attention is set to turn to an International Monetary Fund/World Bank summit, which begins on Saturday and runs through the following week. On the data front, the week is relatively light, with a smattering of Japanese and U.S. figures likely to be the main features.
"The first and obvious focus is the FOMC," said George Magnus, senior international economist at UBS. "The U.S. market is pretty much priced for a modest rise in the funds rate."

Elizabeth Legge, senior economist at Bankgesellschaft Berlin, said an increase of 25 basis points in the federal funds rate, currently 5.25 percent, would not have a major impact on markets given the degree to which it has been discounted.
"If more, it might have some impact on the dollar but I'm not even sure of that because the dollar has got so geared up for a hike," she said.
Bal Sandhu, European strategist at Kleinwort Benson, said Wall Street and European stock markets, which have been bullish, as well as the dollar, all were in state of pre-FOMC tension.
"That's going to be the driving force. It's all going to revolve around whether Wall Street can take any prospective rate hike on the chin," he said.

The big issue at the weekend Ecofin meeting is a so-called Stability Pact, which many analysts expect will be agreed in some form. The pact is designed to set sanctions to ensure countries continue to observe strict fiscal criteria after EMU begins.
But as with the FOMC meeting, analysts said a great deal of the EMU saga has been absorbed by markets.
"European markets have got a lot of this already in their sails," said Magnus, noting how so many European bond spreads were trading at or near historic lows against Bund yields.
"Maybe the markets would respond in a negative way if the stability pact emerged without any teeth, but the word is that there will be some form of (fiscal) provisions," Magnus said.

"The strong performance of the European markets of the last three to four weeks is in contrast to the U.S. and it reflects that the markets are taking EMU even more seriously than they were before," he said.
Britain has a monetary meeting scheduled for Monday but analysts say there is next to no chance of an interest rate cut after data showing vibrant consumer activity in the past week.
Final second quarter gross domestic product data are due on Tuesday for Britain, followed by trade figures on Thursday.
The U.S. has existing home sales for August on Wednesday, durable goods on Thursday and final Q2 GDP on Friday.
In Japan, Friday will be a big day with consumer price, unemployment and retail sales statistics all scheduled.

But analysts said that with authorities keeping a lid on call money rates, the market appears immune to anything other than GDP data or the closely watched "tankan" survey by the Bank of Japan, neither of which are due.
"As long as the economic numbers are reasonably in line with expectations the impact will be fairly small," Legge said.
